title: Vehicles with forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking have 49% fewer front-to-rear crashes in U.S. police data, and pickups with automatic braking have 43% lower rear-end crash rates, 16 November 2022
summary: In U.S. police-reported crash data, forward collision warning with automatic emergency braking cut front-to-rear crashes by 49%, and automatic braking cut pickup rear-end crash rates by 43%.
headline: Crash warning and automatic braking cut front-to-rear crashes by 49%
metric: front-to-rear crashes were reduced by 49%
brief: In a final rule of 9 May 2024, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) required automatic emergency braking on new light vehicles in the United States from September 2029. It found that the systems had reduced injuries and saved lives.[1] On 16 November 2022, VOA Learning English reported that PARTS, a partnership of automakers and NHTSA, had found 49% fewer front-to-rear crashes when the striking vehicle had both forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking. It also reported that the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) had found a 43% lower rear-end crash rate for pickups with automatic emergency braking.[2] In the peer-reviewed version of the IIHS study, Jessica Cicchino found in her main analysis that automatic emergency braking was associated with a 34% lower risk of rear-end-striking crashes.[3] In a second study, published on 6 January 2025 and covering model years 2015 to 2023, PARTS again measured a 49% reduction in front-to-rear crashes.[4] The estimates cover the whole system. They do not separate the camera and radar software from the brakes or from the driver who responds to the warning. False positives in Nissan's automatic emergency braking have posed traffic risks to drivers.

deployer: Multiple automakers (factory-fitted systems)

title: Baricitinib, identified with BenevolentAI's knowledge graph, lowered COVID-19 deaths in the RECOVERY trial
summary: BenevolentAI researchers used the Benevolent Platform's knowledge graph to identify baricitinib for COVID-19, and in the RECOVERY trial mortality was 12% with the drug and 14% with usual care alone.
headline: Drug found with a knowledge graph lowered COVID-19 deaths in a trial
metric: mortality was 12% with the drug and 14% with usual care alone
brief: On 4 February 2020 BenevolentAI researchers reported in The Lancet that their knowledge graph had helped them identify baricitinib, an arthritis drug, as a possible treatment for COVID-19. In the ACTT-2 trial, 1,033 hospitalized adults received remdesivir with either baricitinib or a placebo, and median recovery took 7 days with baricitinib and 8 days with the placebo. In the COV-BARRIER trial, 8% of patients receiving baricitinib had died by day 28, compared with 13% receiving a placebo. Mortality was a secondary outcome in that trial, which did not meet its primary outcome of reduced disease progression.[1] In the later RECOVERY trial, 8,156 patients were randomly assigned to usual care with or without baricitinib, and mortality, its primary outcome, was 12% with baricitinib and 14% with usual care alone.[2] On 14 January 2022 the World Health Organization strongly recommended baricitinib with corticosteroids for patients with severe or critical COVID-19. On 10 May 2022 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved baricitinib for hospitalized adults with COVID-19 who need supplemental oxygen or other respiratory support. In Europe, Eli Lilly withdrew its application on 7 December 2022 after the European Medicines Agency reached the provisional opinion that three trials did not conclusively show meaningful benefit.[3] None of the trials compared discovery with AI against discovery without it, and the knowledge graph's part in the choice rests on a letter and a methods paper by BenevolentAI researchers.[4]

summary: An Embrace wristband detected a seizure that left Morgan McGrath, 26, of Fulton, Missouri, not breathing and alerted her mother, who called paramedics; IEEE Spectrum reports that she survived.
headline: *Embrace* wristband alerts a mother, and she calls paramedics
brief: In November 2016 Morgan McGrath, a 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri, had an epileptic seizure that left her unresponsive and not breathing.[1] Her Embrace wristband detected the seizure and alerted her mother, who called paramedics. McGrath survived, and her rescue rests on a single IEEE Spectrum report. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared the device on 26 January 2018, after the event.[2] Later evidence comes from hospital epilepsy monitoring units. In an independent study published on 7 January 2026, researchers in Montreal found that the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures that occurred while it was worn and working, with 29 false alarms in 373 days of monitoring. It detected none of 510 focal seizures without convulsions, a type that the device is not cleared to detect.[3]

headline: Fitbit flags a racing heart, and doctors treat ventricular tachycardia
metric: detected an irregular heart rate of 164 beats per minute with irregular rhythm
brief: In October 2021 a 55-year-old man in Jamshedpur, India, had symptoms at work, and his Fitbit Sense showed an irregular rhythm at 164 beats per minute. He felt the need to visit a doctor immediately and went to Tata Main Hospital, where cardiologists diagnosed idiopathic fascicular ventricular tachycardia from a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) and further tests. They restored sinus rhythm by electrical cardioversion, and on verapamil he was later reported to be doing well.[1] The U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared the watch's ECG app to tell atrial fibrillation from sinus rhythm, and ventricular tachycardia lies outside the rhythms that it was cleared to classify.[2] The benefit also rests on an assumption that he would have waited longer without the reading, and a single case report gives no way to check it.

title: ASENA analysis program flags a car at Yüksekova carrying 52.5 kg of explosives bound for Istanbul
summary: The Turkish police's ASENA analysis program flagged a car at Yüksekova on 20 March 2022, and officers found 52.5 kg of explosives that the interior minister said were bound for Istanbul.
headline: ASENA flags a car at Yüksekova carrying 52.5 kg of explosives
metric: 133 packets, 52.5 kg, of factory-made explosive
brief: On 20 March 2022 officers of the Hakkari Provincial Police Directorate stopped a car at a checkpoint in Yüksekova, Turkey, after work on the directorate's ASENA analysis program had flagged it. A hidden compartment under the spare-wheel well held 133 packets, 52.5 kg in all, of factory-made explosive assessed as PETN-RDX.[1] The driver was a police officer posted in Istanbul, and on 20 November 2023 the Hakkari 2nd Heavy Penal Court sentenced him to 21 years in prison and four co-defendants to 17.5 years each for supplying weapons to a terrorist organization.[2] ASENA was built to flag drug crime, so this find lay outside its purpose. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu said on 21 March 2022 that police using analysis programs, “what they call artificial intelligence”, had identified a suspicious vehicle thought to be carrying drugs.[3] In June 2022 the head of the police Narcotics Crimes Department listed the explosives among the finds of operations that, by his account, had started with ASENA.[4] No source describes the data that ASENA matched for this car or whether an analyst checked the flag before the stop. The driver spoke in court of “those who informed”, but no source reports an informant.[5]
system: ASENA (Analiz Sistemleri Narkotik Ağı), Turkish National Police narcotics analysis software
